<h1>
  <img src="brand/docs-studio-mark.svg"
       width="55"
       height="55"
       align="absmiddle"
       alt="ARIS.jl icon">
  docs-studio
</h1>

Generate polished [Zensical](https://zensical.org) documentation sites from one config
file.

**Documentation: <https://lea-m-hadzic.github.io/docs-studio/>** — generated by
`docs-studio` itself, from [`docs-studio.toml`](docs-studio.toml) in this repository.

The design language is extracted from two documentation sites that are in production —
[wm-physics-eval](https://sisl.github.io/wm-physics-eval/) and
[ARIS.jl](https://sisl.github.io/ARIS.jl/) — so a generated site looks like those
rather than like a default theme: semantic colour tokens mapped onto the theme's own
variables, a hairline above each section, a wider article beside a narrow "On this
page", compact outlined resource buttons on the home page, and matching light and dark
schemes that are checked against WCAG AA before anything is written.

A generated site makes **no third-party requests**: system fonts, no CDN, no web font,
no maths renderer.

## Install

`docs-studio` is not published to PyPI, so install it from a clone:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/lea-m-hadzic/docs-studio
cd docs-studio
uv sync
uv run docs-studio --help
```

To use it outside this checkout, build a wheel and install that:

```bash
uv build
uv tool install dist/docs_studio-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
```

(Once it is published, `uv tool install docs-studio` or `pipx install docs-studio`
will do.)

Zensical itself is optional. `init` and `check` work without it; `check` then skips the
build step and says so. To build and preview:

```bash
pip install "zensical==0.0.67"
```

## Use

```bash
docs-studio init my-docs \
  --name "my-package" \
  --description "What it does, in one line" \
  --author "Your Lab" \
  --repo-url https://github.com/org/my-package \
  --language python \
  --preset ocean-violet \
  --yes

cd my-docs
docs-studio check
zensical serve
```

`init` is interactive without `--yes`, and fully scriptable with it. It runs in a new
directory or in an existing repository, and never overwrites a file that is already
there unless you pass `--force`.

Then write the pages. `docs/*.md` are starters, each carrying a marker comment;
`docs-studio check` lists every page that still has one, and
`--require-authored` turns that into a failure so an unwritten page cannot ship.

## The three commands

### `init`

Writes `docs-studio.toml`, `zensical.toml`, the stylesheet, the starter pages, the
artwork, and (optionally) the GitHub Pages workflow. With no logo supplied it generates
a monogram from the project's initials and the palette, in both light and dark
variants, and wires up the dark-mode swap.

### `check`

Validates what can be validated without publishing, in three layers:

- **universal** — the config parses; the nav and the page set are a bijection, with no
  duplicates and nothing orphaned; every internal link and heading anchor resolves;
  referenced assets exist, including the dark logo that is referenced from CSS rather
  than from the config; no absolute path that would 404 under a GitHub Pages sub-path;
  no unrendered template syntax; the palette clears WCAG AA in **both** schemes.
- **language-specific** — code fences carry a language the profile expects, and fences
  are parsed where a real parser exists: Python with `ast`, TOML with `tomllib`, JSON
  with `json`.
- **the build** — `zensical build --clean --strict`, when Zensical is installed.

Every diagnostic carries a file and, where it has one, a line. Errors exit 1.

What `check` deliberately does *not* do is compare the docs against your code. Whether
a documented function exists, whether a documented default matches the source, whether
a snippet produces the output shown — that needs to import your project, so it belongs
in your own test suite. Both reference repositories do exactly that, and it is worth
copying: see [docs/validation.md](docs/validation.md) for the two patterns.

### `update`

Regenerates the managed styling and config when you change the palette or upgrade the
toolkit, without touching your content.

```bash
docs-studio update --dry-run    # the full plan and diffs, writes nothing
docs-studio update              # asks before writing
```

Every generated file is recorded in `.docs-studio/manifest.json` with a sha256 and an
ownership:

| | on disk | what `update` does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| managed | absent | creates it |
| managed | unchanged since generated | replaces it if the render differs |
| managed | **edited** | **conflict** — reported, skipped, never overwritten |
| managed | not in the manifest | **conflict** — it did not write it, so it will not take it over |
| seeded | absent | creates it (this is how a page added to the nav appears) |
| seeded | present | leaves it alone, always |

`docs/stylesheets/custom.css` is seeded, which is what makes it a safe place for your
own CSS — see [Your own CSS](#your-own-css).

A skipped conflict keeps its old recorded hash, so it stays a conflict until someone
resolves it. `--force` applies conflicts too and is the only way to lose an edit.

## Configuration

`docs-studio.toml` is the only file you are expected to edit. It is written with its
own documentation in the comments. The essentials:

```toml
[project]
name = "my-package"
description = "What it does, in one line"
author = "Your Lab"
site_url = "https://org.github.io/my-package/"   # includes the Pages sub-path
repo_url = "https://github.com/org/my-package"
language = "python"                               # python | julia | generic

[theme]
preset = "ocean-violet"                           # see `docs-studio presets`

# Override individual tokens on top of the preset:
# [theme.light]
# primary = "#4B5FD7"
# [theme.dark]
# primary = "#7E8FFF"

[branding]
logo = "docs/assets/my-logo.svg"                  # copied verbatim; never overwritten
# logo_dark = "docs/assets/my-logo-dark.svg"
# wordmark  = "docs/assets/my-wordmark.svg"
# favicon   = "docs/assets/favicon.ico"

[[resources]]
label = "GitHub Repository"
url = "https://github.com/org/my-package"
icon = "simple-github"                            # or image = "assets/logo.svg"

[[nav]]
title = "Home"
page = "index.md"

[[nav]]
title = "Getting started"
pages = ["quickstart.md", { title = "Installation", page = "install.md" }]

[deploy]
github_pages = true
trigger = "manual"                                # manual | push
zensical_version = "0.0.67"                       # pinned, so a build is reproducible
```

No secrets go in this file. The Pages workflow needs none: it authenticates with the
workflow's own OIDC token.

## Your own CSS

Every site gets `docs/stylesheets/custom.css`, generated once and then left alone
forever. It is listed in `extra_css` **after** the design-system stylesheet, so at
equal specificity anything in it wins:

```toml
extra_css = ["stylesheets/extra.css", "stylesheets/custom.css"]
```

Put additions and overrides there rather than in `extra.css`, which is managed and
would report your edit as a conflict. Editing `custom.css` is never a conflict;
changing the palette, the templates or the toolkit version leaves it exactly as you
left it, and `--force` does not reach it either.

The design tokens are already defined for both schemes, so prefer them over literal
colours and your rules follow light and dark on their own:

```css
/* docs/stylesheets/custom.css */
.md-typeset .lead {
  color: var(--ds-muted);
  font-size: 0.9rem;
}
```

A site generated before this file existed picks it up on the next
`docs-studio update`, and a `custom.css` you already had is kept, not replaced.

## Palettes

```bash
docs-studio presets
```

| preset | from | character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `indigo-lavender` | ARIS.jl | violet links, lavender in dark mode, coral as a restrained accent |
| `ocean-violet` | wm-physics-eval | one blue-violet accent on cool neutrals, muted amber for warnings |
| `neutral` | — | desaturated slate and a quiet sage accent; no brand colour of its own |

A palette is twelve required tokens per scheme (`primary`, `primary_hover`,
`on_primary`, `secondary`, `accent`, `fg`, `fg_body`, `muted`, `border`, `bg`,
`surface`, `surface_alt`) plus six that are derived if you leave them out
(`primary_tint`, `accent_text`, `accent_tint`, `bg_translucent`, `link`, `link_hover`).

`accent_text` is the one worth knowing about. A brand accent is often too light to be
read as text — ARIS's coral `#F0787F` is 2.7:1 on white — so `accent` stays decorative
and `accent_text` is darkened or lightened automatically until it clears 4.5:1 against
that scheme's background. Contrast is validated for every text pair in both schemes
before any file is written; a custom palette that fails is reported, not shipped.

Supply a whole palette of your own with `theme.palette_file = "my-palette.toml"`, or
override individual tokens with `[theme.light]` / `[theme.dark]`.

## Deployment

With `github_pages = true`, `init` writes `.github/workflows/docs.yml`: minimal
permissions (`contents: read`, `pages: write`, `id-token: write`), the checker, a
strict build, `upload-pages-artifact`, `deploy-pages`. `trigger = "manual"` emits
`workflow_dispatch` only, so nothing publishes until someone asks; `trigger = "push"`
adds the push trigger for your default branch.

One-time setup, which has to be done by hand: in the repository's **Settings → Pages**,
set **Source** to **GitHub Actions**. Until then the deploy step fails with "Pages site
not found".

docs-studio does not create repositories, change repository settings, push, or deploy.

## Project layout of a generated site

```
docs-studio.toml              your settings — the only file you edit
zensical.toml                 managed
docs/
  index.md  quickstart.md …   seeded once, then yours
  stylesheets/extra.css       managed — the generated design system
  stylesheets/custom.css      yours — your CSS goes here
  assets/                     yours; never overwritten
.github/workflows/docs.yml    managed
.docs-studio/manifest.json    ownership and checksums — commit this
site/                         build output; add to .gitignore
```

Commit `.docs-studio/manifest.json`. Without it, `update` cannot tell a generated file
from an edited one and treats everything managed as a conflict.

## Development

```bash
uv sync
uv run pytest
uv run docs-studio --help
```

This repository's own documentation site is generated by the toolkit, so it is also a
test of it:

```bash
uv run docs-studio check          # validates docs/ and builds it strictly
uv run docs-studio update --dry-run
```

See [docs/contributing.md](docs/contributing.md).
